title: Static Equilibrium Problems
short: For ladders, hinged beams and hanging signs, choose a pivot that removes the unknowns you don't need.
trouble: Students think a hinge's force on a beam must point along the beam.

blocks.html: Rotational Equilibrium set the two conditions for an object at rest: zero net force and zero net torque about any point. With Static Friction and the vector torques of Torque as a Cross Product, you can solve ladders, hinged beams and hanging signs. The Book Cart lab lets you feel what happens when the balance fails.

For a rigid body in equilibrium: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$ about any point. Choose the pivot where the most unknown forces act: their torques vanish, often leaving one equation with one unknown.

If the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point: moving the pivot by $\vec{a}$ changes each $\vec{r}$ to $\vec{r} - \vec{a}$, and the total torque changes by $-\vec{a}\times\sum\vec{F} = 0$. So you are free to pick the most convenient point. A force through the pivot has zero lever arm, so it drops out of the torque equation, which is how a smart choice removes unknowns you don't need.

blocks.name: ph-torque

opts.task: Move the painter up the ladder and watch the friction needed at the floor grow.

blocks.cap: A ladder against a frictionless wall. The floor's friction must balance the wall's push, and the torque balance about the foot sets how big that push is.

blocks.title: A ladder
blocks.q: A uniform $15\ \text{kg}$, $4.0\ \text{m}$ ladder leans against a frictionless wall at $60^\circ$ above the floor. Find the friction needed at the floor, and the least $\mu_s$.
steps: Forces: wall push $N_w$ (horizontal), floor normal $N_f$ (up), floor friction $f$ (toward the wall), weight $mg$ at the middle.
Torques about the foot (removes $N_f$ and $f$): $N_wL\sin 60^\circ = mg\tfrac{L}{2}\cos 60^\circ$, so $N_w = \dfrac{mg}{2\tan 60^\circ} = \dfrac{147}{3.46} = 42.4\ \text{N}$.

blocks.title: A sign on a hinged beam
blocks.q: A uniform $20\ \text{kg}$, $3.0\ \text{m}$ beam sticks out from a wall on a hinge, held by a cable from its far end at $30^\circ$ to the beam. A $40\ \text{kg}$ sign hangs at the far end. Find the cable tension and the hinge force.
steps: Horizontal: the hinge pushes out with $H_x = T\cos 30^\circ = 849\ \text{N}$.

blocks.html: Assuming the hinge's force points along the beam. That's only true for a light rod with forces at its two ends alone. A beam carrying its own weight and a load needs the hinge to push both outward and (usually) upward. Check: after finding $T$ from torques, write both force equations; if $H_y$ comes out nonzero, the hinge force is tilted off the beam's line.
